item.description:
Zug leaves as soon as you answer, and the coloured bar beside him is gone.
## Zug goes when the question does
The robot in the notch used to stay after the work did. He turned green and stood still when an agent finished its turn, and red with a dark antenna when one died — both of them news about something that had already stopped, sitting in the notch until a timer took it away.
Now he is there only while an agent is actually waiting on you. Answer the permission prompt — Approve, Always, or Reject — and he leaves at once, because the thing he was asking about is over. There is no green Zug and no red one any more; the only Zug is the one waving for an answer.
The sound is unchanged and was always this way: two rising blips when a request lands, and never for anything else.
Nothing is lost. The strip under the board still lists every session — working, finished, ended — with what each one was doing and how long ago. That is where news belongs. The notch is for what you still owe someone.
## The coloured bar is gone
The right side of the closed pill also lit a small capsule for the game itself: green for your move, red for check or a finished game. 0.7.5 put a fuse on it so it would stop being lit all the time. This release takes it out instead.
It was restating the mascot an inch away. The dino is blue when there is no game, green when there is one, and sorry-looking when you have lost — a bar beside it in a second palette is two things to read where there was one. And a mark that lights for every move of every game drifts back toward being a lamp whatever fuse is on it.
So the closed pill now says exactly one thing, and says it only while it is true: somebody is blocked on you. The rest of the time there is just the animal, and whether a game is on.

A robot called Zug now lives in the notch, and the light beside the mascot stops being on all the time.
## A robot called Zug
When Claude Code or Codex stops and asks for permission, the right side of the pill now grows a small pixel robot. It waves, it hops, and the light on its antenna blinks while it waits for you. Answer the request and it goes.
It is called Zug, after Zugzwang — the position where you are obliged to move. That is the whole of what it stands for: something has stopped, and it cannot go on until you answer.
It also has a voice: two rising blips, about a quarter of a second, the moment the request lands. The robot only works if you are looking at the notch, and nobody waiting on a permission prompt is — you are looking at the terminal that just went quiet, usually on another screen. The sound is the half of the signal that reaches you there. Turn it off with Settings ▸ Sounds, along with every other sound the app makes.
The robot answers for the other two agent states as well, in colour rather than in movement: green and standing still when an agent has finished its turn, red with its antenna dark when one has died. Only a blocked agent waves, and only a blocked agent makes a sound — a finished agent is not made more finished by jumping up and down.
Everything the robot replaces was a coloured bar. A chess mark comments on the board you are already looking at; an agent is a different machine in a different window, and a shape carries that difference from across the desk in a way a colour cannot.
## The light stops being on all the time
The green mark for "your move" was lit whenever a game existed — and a game exists from the moment the app launches, because it restores the last one or starts a fresh board. So the mark was on over an untouched home screen, and it stayed on for as long as a half-finished game sat there, which for most people meant permanently.
It is now a call rather than a state. Every move lights it, and it goes out about three quarters of a minute after the last thing that happened — so it is up for the whole of a game you are playing, and dark on a board you have walked away from. The next move brings it back.
The mascot is unchanged and still says whether a game is on: blue with no game, green with one, whether or not the mark beside it has anything to add.

The buttons under the board sit evenly again.
## Hint stops holding a gap open
The Hint button used to count: press it once and it read "Hint 1/3", again for "Hint 2/3", and so on round the three moves it offers. To keep Undo and Resign from sliding sideways as that caption grew, the row reserved room for the widest version of it from the moment the board opened — so before you pressed anything there was a gap in front of Undo about twice the size of the one after it.
The count is gone and so is the reserved room. Every button now takes exactly the width of its own label, and the spacing between Hint, Undo and Resign is the same all the way across.
Nothing about the hint itself changed. It still offers three candidate moves at the position you are in, still moves to the next one each time you press, still wraps round to the first after the third, and still never runs out while the position stands.

The notch stops looking like it is recording you, and puzzle pieces move.
## The light in the notch
The small round lamp on the right side of the pill is gone. It sat in the shape, the size and very nearly the place of the Mac's own camera-in-use indicator, and enough people read it as "this app is watching you" that the shape had to go.
In its place is a short capsule, and it is lit only when you are actually wanted: your move, a check or a finished game, or an agent waiting on an answer. When nothing needs you — idle, or while the engine is thinking — the right ear is simply empty. The mascot still tells the two apart: blue at rest, green once a game is on.
Nothing about what the app can see changed here, because there was never anything to change. Dyno Chess carries no camera, microphone or network entitlement at all, and you can check that yourself in a second:
`codesign -d --entitlements :- '/Applications/Dyno Chess.app'`
## Puzzles play their moves
Puzzle pieces used to change squares between two frames. The board would open with the opponent's move already made, and after a correct answer the reply simply appeared — which meant working out what had happened before you could start working out what to do about it.
Both of those now travel across the board the way the engine's moves always have in a game: the piece lifts, crosses, and sets down, and a captured piece stays whole long enough to watch it go. Your own moves are not replayed back at you.
If you have Reduce Motion switched on in System Settings, the board stays instant — as it should.
## The panel opens in two beats
Hovering the island used to play one chord: the notch sprang open while the panel faded in on the same spring, re-laying out the board at every width the spring passed through. What that looked like was the content squeezing itself into place from the right while the notch was still moving.
Now the panel is laid out once at its final size and the notch grows to uncover it, so the shape opens and *then* the panel arrives. Closing is the mirror: the panel leaves first and the notch closes over the space.
## The home screen says which game
The result card above New Game used to read "Checkmate · Black wins" with no indication of which game it meant — awkward on a screen you also walk back to mid-session. It now carries a "LAST GAME" label and how long ago it finished, kept true on the minute rather than written once and left to rot.
The stats beside it became three rings over one denominator, which shows the win/draw/loss split before you read a digit. No win rate is shown until something has actually been decided; an all-hot-seat history used to read as a losing streak that never happened.
